account: On 30 September 2026, Gianluca Inguglia, Huw Haigh and Ulyana Dupletsa posted a paper on arXiv. They are at the Marietta Blau Institute for Particle Physics (Austrian Academy of Sciences, Vienna). Alessandro Longo (University of Urbino and INFN Florence) is a co-author. The paper is titled “MADGRAV: a multilevel anomaly-detection pipeline for gravitational-wave searches applied to LIGO data”. Version 2 followed on 19 October 2026, and the paper is submitted to the European Physical Journal C. The pipeline is “a series of sequential convolutional neural networks that perform anomaly detection, glitch classification, coherence testing, and signal ranking”. It is applied to one-second Q-transform windows of data from the Hanford and Livingston detectors in the observing runs O3a, O3b, O4a and O4b. That is 442.9 days of coincident livetime in total. The abstract reports 47 detections with a false alarm rate below one per year and p_astro above 0.9, where p_astro is the probability of astrophysical origin. Of those, “44 are shared with the minimally modelled coherent WaveBurst search”. The three others are cataloged events, and the authors state that “no candidate without a catalog counterpart survives the analysis”. Recovery rises with mass. It reaches 8.1% of confident catalog events below 30 solar masses and 39.8% between 30 and 100. It reaches 53.3% above 100 for a network signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) above 10. The authors conclude that anomaly-detection pipelines “can serve as an independent detection channel complementary to matched filtering in the high-mass high-SNR regime”. The paper confirms no new event independently. The authors identify the two-detector configuration as MADGRAV-2D in their code repository. Its changelog dates the final pipeline configuration to 14 September 2026, and its README states that this configuration produced the reported 47 detections. The repository provides the trained weights and frozen calibration. It already records the 47 detections in a commit dated 1 September 2026. The final configuration keeps the same 47, and 42 of them reach a p_astro of 0.99 or more. As of 29 October 2026 the paper is still under submission, and INSPIRE-HEP lists no paper that cites it.

fields.account: On 30 September 2026, Gianluca Inguglia, Huw Haigh and Ulyana Dupletsa posted a paper on arXiv. They are at the Marietta Blau Institute for Particle Physics (Austrian Academy of Sciences, Vienna). Alessandro Longo (University of Urbino and INFN Florence) is a co-author. The paper is titled “MADGRAV: a multilevel anomaly-detection pipeline for gravitational-wave searches applied to LIGO data”. Version 2 followed on 19 October 2026, and the paper is submitted to the European Physical Journal C. The pipeline is “a series of sequential convolutional neural networks that perform anomaly detection, glitch classification, coherence testing, and signal ranking”. It is applied to one-second Q-transform windows of data from the Hanford and Livingston detectors in the observing runs O3a, O3b, O4a and O4b. That is 442.9 days of coincident livetime in total. The abstract reports 47 detections with a false alarm rate below one per year and p_astro above 0.9, where p_astro is the probability of astrophysical origin. Of those, “44 are shared with the minimally modelled coherent WaveBurst search”. The three others are cataloged events, and the authors state that “no candidate without a catalog counterpart survives the analysis”. Recovery rises with mass. It reaches 8.1% of confident catalog events below 30 solar masses and 39.8% between 30 and 100. It reaches 53.3% above 100 for a network signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) above 10. The authors conclude that anomaly-detection pipelines “can serve as an independent detection channel complementary to matched filtering in the high-mass high-SNR regime”. The paper confirms no new event independently. The authors identify the two-detector configuration as MADGRAV-2D in their code repository. Its changelog dates the final pipeline configuration to 14 September 2026, and its README states that this configuration produced the reported 47 detections. The repository provides the trained weights and frozen calibration. It already records the 47 detections in a commit dated 1 September 2026. The final configuration keeps the same 47, and 42 of them reach a p_astro of 0.99 or more. As of 29 October 2026 the paper is still under submission, and INSPIRE-HEP lists no paper that cites it.
